h1: The 7 Best NAS Drives for Photo and Video Storage, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best NAS for Photo and Video: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 NAS units for photo and video libraries, scored on bays, CPU, RAM, 2.5GbE speed, RAID options and software.
mainKeyword: best nas for photo and video storage
summary: The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is the best NAS for a large and growing photo and video archive, with four bays, RAID 5 and a five-core Pentium Gold. The TERRAMASTER F2-425 is the pick for editors on a 2-bay budget, QNAP's TS-264-8G brings 8GB of RAM, and Synology's DS223 has the easiest software.
intro: Most people buy a NAS for capacity and discover the real limit is the network cable. A 1GbE port tops out around 110 MB/s, which is fine for browsing photos and painful when you scrub through 4K footage on the share. A big case with a slow port is a very expensive way to wait, and the problem is invisible on the product page.

We ranked seven NAS units from listing data, weighing bay count, CPU, RAM, networking speed, RAID support and software. Drives are sold separately on every model, so budget for two or four disks, ideally NAS-rated, on top of the chassis price. If you edit video from the share, give networking and CPU the most weight; for photo backup alone, bay count and software matter more.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DXP4800 Plus 4-Bay
products.verdict: Four bays, RAID 5 and a Pentium Gold 8505 give a growing library room to breathe.
products.description:
The DXP4800 Plus is a 4-bay diskless NAS built on an Intel Pentium Gold 8505 with five cores. It supports RAID 5, which spreads parity across the drives so one can fail without losing data, and it expands to far more total capacity than any 2-bay unit here.

It ranks first because photo and video libraries only grow. A 2-bay box mirrors two drives and wastes half of them, while four bays under RAID 5 give you more usable space and the same single-drive safety. The faster processor also matters when you want the NAS to transcode 4K clips for playback on a phone.

It is the unit for a working photographer or a family with years of footage. The tradeoff is cost: it sits in the $500+ bucket before you add drives, and a 2-bay model is enough if your archive is under a few terabytes.
products.idealFor: Photographers and families with large, growing photo and video archives.
products.skipIf: Your library is small and fits two drives.

products.name: TERRAMASTER F2-425 2-Bay NAS
products.verdict: An Intel x86 quad-core, 4GB of RAM and 2.5GbE in a 2-bay chassis.
products.description:
The TERRAMASTER F2-425 is a diskless 2-bay NAS with an Intel x86 quad-core CPU, 4GB of RAM and a 2.5GbE port, plus multimedia server support. It is the most capable 2-bay processor in the group.

It outranks the QNAP TS-264 on CPU grounds, since x86 processors handle video transcoding well, while the QNAP counters with more RAM. Against the DXP4800 Plus it gives up the extra bays and RAID 5, but it saves a large chunk of money and still delivers faster-than-gigabit transfers.

Editors who proxy-edit video off the NAS will notice the 2.5GbE link, provided their computer has a 2.5GbE port too. The limit is 4GB of RAM and two bays: heavy multi-user work or a large archive will outgrow it.
products.idealFor: Video editors who want transcoding power in a 2-bay box.
products.skipIf: You expect to add drives later.

products.name: QNAP TS-264-8G 2-Bay Desktop NAS
products.verdict: 8GB of RAM included gives active editing and multitasking a larger working pool.
products.description:
The QNAP TS-264-8G is a 2-bay desktop NAS that ships with 8GB of RAM, running QNAP's QTS platform. Drives are sold separately.

It ranks third because RAM is useful when several people stream, sync and back up at once, and 8GB is twice the TERRAMASTER's 4GB. QNAP's QTS is feature-rich, with a deeper app list than the lean consumer-oriented interfaces, which is a strength for experienced buyers and a learning curve for newcomers.

Buy it if you want to stay with a 2-bay chassis but expect heavy use. The listing does not state the networking speed in our data, so confirm port speed before you buy a switch or cable to match.
products.idealFor: Editors and power users who run many services at once.
products.skipIf: You want the simplest possible setup.

products.name: Synology DS223 2-Bay NAS
products.verdict: Synology's DSM is the easiest, most mature interface for managing a photo archive.
products.description:
The DS223 is a 2-bay diskless NAS aimed at home and small office backup, running Synology DSM with a focus on centralized file protection. It uses standard 1GbE networking.

It lands fourth because the hardware is modest next to the 2.5GbE rivals. What it buys you is software maturity: DSM is widely regarded as the cleanest NAS interface, with a polished photo app and reliable backup tools. For people who value a calm setup over spec numbers, that is worth the lower rating.

Buy it if you will mostly store and back up photos rather than edit video from the share. A single gigabit link caps transfers, so large video projects will feel slow compared with the 2.5GbE units.
products.idealFor: Photo archivists who want the easiest management software.
products.skipIf: You edit video directly from the NAS.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DXP2800 2-Bay
products.verdict: A 2-bay with RAID 1 mirroring for creators leaving external USB drives behind.
products.description:
The DXP2800 is a 2-bay diskless NAS positioned at creators and enthusiasts. It supports RAID 1 mirroring and uses standard 1GbE networking.

It ranks fifth because it carries a creator-friendly feature set but the gigabit link caps video throughput. Against the Asustor Drivestor 2 Gen 2 below, it gives up 2.5GbE, while the Asustor sits in a lower price bucket. RAID 1 is the key: two drives hold identical copies, so a failed disk does not take your photos with it.

It is a good first NAS if you are moving off a USB drive. The 1GbE port tops out around 110 MB/s, fine for photos and fine for streaming, but slow for large video work.
products.idealFor: Solo creators leaving external USB drives for the first time.

products.name: Asustor Drivestor 2 Gen 2 AS1202T
products.verdict: The cheapest way to 2.5GbE, with a quad-core 1.7GHz CPU and 4K media serving.
products.description:
Asustor's AS1202T packs two bays, a 1.7GHz four-core processor, 1GB of DDR4 and a 2.5GbE port into the budget tier, and it can serve 4K media.

Sixth place follows from the memory: 1GB of RAM is thin for demanding sync and transcode tasks, and the CPU is a notch below the Intel-based picks. In return it is the cheapest unit that still has a 2.5GbE port, which gives a real speed lift if your computer has a matching connection.

Buy it for photo libraries and light 4K playback on a budget. Skip it if you plan to run several apps at once, since 1GB of memory is the first thing you will run out of.
products.idealFor: Budget buyers who want faster-than-gigabit transfers.
products.skipIf: You plan to run many apps.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DH2300 2-Bay
products.verdict: A budget 2-bay that supports up to 64TB total capacity.
products.description:
The DH2300 is a compact 2-bay desktop NAS that supports up to 64TB of total capacity, with a budget-tier processor and networking. It is priced at the entry level.

Last place reflects its processor and network are entry-level, so it is built to store, not to transcode. The 64TB ceiling is the number to notice: two large drives give a roomy archive for the price, which suits photos you rarely touch.

Pick it for a cold archive or a family photo backup. It is the wrong tool for editing or heavy streaming, so use the TERRAMASTER or DXP4800 Plus for that.
products.idealFor: Family photo backups and cold archives on a budget.
products.skipIf: You edit or stream 4K video from it.

methodology.title: Bay count and RAID
methodology.description: How many drives the chassis takes and what protection it supports.

methodology.title: Processor
methodology.description: CPU class for transcoding photos and video for playback.

methodology.title: Network speed
methodology.description: 1GbE versus 2.5GbE, which decides editing from the share.

methodology.title: Memory
methodology.description: RAM included for sync, indexing and multiple users.

methodology.title: Software
methodology.description: The management ecosystem and photo tools around the hardware.

whatMatters.detail: Bay count sets how many drives the NAS holds and what RAID level you can run. A 2-bay mirrors drives with RAID 1, so half your disk space goes to redundancy, while a 4-bay with RAID 5 loses only one drive's worth. Read the listing for supported RAID levels. RAID protects against a drive dying, not deletion or theft, so it never replaces a backup.

CPU decides whether the NAS can transcode, which is converting big video files on the fly for a phone or TV. x86 chips like the TERRAMASTER's Intel quad-core or the DXP4800 Plus's Pentium Gold handle it far better than low-end processors. Without enough CPU, playback stutters on weak devices. Look for the processor name and core count in the specs.

2.5GbE moves roughly 280 MB/s against 110 MB/s for gigabit, but the speed only appears if your computer and switch also support it. Plug a 2.5GbE NAS into a gigabit switch and you get gigabit. Check the NAS port spec, then check the other end of the cable. The Synology DS223 and UGREEN DXP2800 list 1GbE, and the TERRAMASTER lists 2.5GbE.

RAM handles indexing, sync clients, photo apps and containers at once, and starved memory makes the whole box feel slow. The QNAP TS-264 ships with 8GB, the TERRAMASTER 4GB and the Asustor 1GB. Look for the RAM figure on the listing, and check whether it is upgradeable, because some designs solder or restrict memory and leave you stuck with the number you bought.

The software is what you live with every day: photo apps, mobile backup, sharing permissions and snapshots. Synology DSM is the most polished for beginners, QNAP QTS the deepest for power users. A confusing interface means people skip setting up scheduled backups, which is the entire point of the device. Check the operating system by name and read a few setup reviews.

cards.label: 4-bay
cards.text: Costs more, offers RAID 5 and more capacity. Pick: UGREEN DXP4800 Plus.

howToChoose.note: Buy 4-bay if you will outgrow two disks in three years.

faq.a: No. Every unit here is diskless, so budget for two or four NAS-rated drives on top of the chassis price. The DH2300 supports up to 64TB total, which gives a sense of the capacity ceiling for the budget picks.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake buyers make?
faq.a: Buying 2.5GbE hardware and plugging it into a gigabit switch or computer. The TERRAMASTER F2-425 and Asustor AS1202T only run faster if the rest of the chain, including the PC port and the switch, supports 2.5GbE.

faq.q: Is a NAS worth it over cloud storage?
faq.a: For large photo and video libraries, yes. You pay once for hardware, keep local speed and avoid subscription tiers that climb with every terabyte. You should still keep a second copy offsite, since the NAS itself shares the house with the fire risk.

Synology DSM is the gentlest, with guided disk setup and clear menus. QNAP QTS on the TS-264 offers more options and a steeper curve. Plan an evening for either: install the drives, create a RAID volume, then add shared folders and a phone backup.

faq.q: How do I maintain a NAS?
faq.a: Update firmware, run drive health checks and replace a failing disk promptly. With RAID 1 on the DXP2800 or RAID 5 on the DXP4800 Plus, one failure is survivable, not two. Keep a spare drive size noted so a swap does not wait on shopping.

No. RAID protects against a single drive failing, not deletion, a virus, theft or fire. Keep a second copy elsewhere, even if you buy the DXP4800 Plus, and test a restore once so you know the backup actually works.

finalTake: The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is the NAS to buy if your archive will keep growing. The TERRAMASTER F2-425 is the sweet spot for 2-bay editors, and Synology's DS223 suits people who value simple software over speed. Budget for drives, check that your computer supports 2.5GbE before paying for it, and keep one backup off the NAS.
